chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from al-Mukhtar ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mukhtar and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Abdullah ibn al-Hasan al-Alawi, all together from al-Fath ibn Yazeed al-Jurjani, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him)

Regarding four who testified against a man that he had committed adultery, so he was stoned. Then they retracted and said, 'We erred.' They are obligated to pay the blood money (diyah). And if they say, 'We were deliberate,' the guardian of the killed one may kill whichever of the four he wishes. The three (who are killed) pay three-quarters of the blood money to the guardians of the second one killed, and the three are each whipped eighty lashes. And if the guardian of the killed one wishes to kill them all, he pays three blood monies to the guardians of the four witnesses, and they are each whipped eighty lashes, then the Imam kills them.

And he (peace be upon him) said regarding two men who testified against a man that he had stolen, so his hand was cut. Then one of them retracted and said, 'I erred regarding this, but it was someone else.' He is obligated to pay half the blood money of the hand, and his testimony is not accepted regarding the other. If both retract and say, 'We erred, but so-and-so was the thief,' they are both obligated to pay the blood money of the hand, and their testimony is not accepted regarding the other.

And if they say, 'We were deliberate,' the hand of one of the two is cut by the hand of the one whose hand was cut, and the one whose hand was not cut pays a quarter of the blood money of the man to the guardians of the one whose hand was cut. If the first one (whose hand was) cut says, 'I am not pleased until both their hands are cut together,' he returns the blood money of one hand to be divided between them, and both their hands are cut.
ai.seo_question: What is the legal consequence for witnesses who retract their testimony after a punishment has been executed?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the jurisprudential distinction between unintentional error (wahm) and deliberate falsehood (ta'ammud) in witness testimony, a critical nuance in Shia fiqh for determining liability. It details how the Imam or heir of the punished individual may choose between financial compensation (diyah) or execution of the witnesses, reflecting the principle of 'Qasas' (retaliatory justice) applied to legal errors. The text underscores the gravity of bearing false witness, linking it directly to the forfeiture of one's own life or limb in the case of deliberate deceit.
